q: What does a React Native <Text> become on the phone?
options: A real native text view, on Android and on iPhone
A piece of web text inside a hidden browser
A picture of text drawn by JavaScript
A web view that loads an HTML file
why: React Native has no browser inside. Each core component becomes the phone's own view, so the app looks and scrolls like a normal phone app.

q: Which of these are done by the UI thread?
options: Making and updating the real native views
why: The UI thread draws the screen, listens to touches and is the only thread that changes native views. Your onPress and your components run on the JavaScript thread.

q: Put the three steps of the render pipeline in order.
items: Render: React runs your components and the shadow tree is made
Commit: the layout is worked out and the tree becomes the next tree
Mount: the UI thread makes or updates the native views
why: Render, commit, mount. The JavaScript thread does the first two. The UI thread does the last one.

q: Your own App component gets a node in the shadow tree.
why: No. React keeps running your own components until only host parts such as View and Text are left. Only those get shadow nodes.

q: A loop blocks the JavaScript thread for 3 seconds. A user drags a long ScrollView and presses a button. What happens?
options: The list scrolls, but the button does not react until the loop ends
Both the list and the button stop
The button works, but the list is frozen
why: The ScrollView lives on the UI thread, so it scrolls without JavaScript. The button press must reach JavaScript, which is busy.

q: Speed tests must run in a ______ build, not in development mode. (one word)
why: Development mode does a lot of extra checking, so JavaScript is much slower. Test speed in a release build, the version you ship.
